title: Comprehensions
short: Build a list, dict, set or grid in one readable line.
what: A comprehension is a for loop that builds a new collection, written inside brackets: [x * x for x in nums]. Square brackets make a list, curly brackets a set or a dict. An if at the end filters.
analogy: A recipe card that says "for every apple in the basket, slice it, but skip the bruised ones". One sentence instead of a page of steps.

frames.label: nums
frames.say: nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. A comprehension reads it and builds a new collection in one line.

frames.label: [x * x for x in nums]
frames.say: [x * x for x in nums]: for each x, put x * x in the new list. Same as a for loop with append, shorter.

frames.label: [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]
frames.say: An if at the end filters: [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0] keeps only 2 and 4.

frames.label: {x: i for i, x in enumerate(nums)}
frames.say: {x: i for i, x in enumerate(nums)} builds a dict: each value maps to its index. Handy for Two Sum style lookups.

frames.label: {x % 3 for x in nums}
frames.say: {x % 3 for x in nums} is a set: 1, 2, 0, 1, 2 collapses to {0, 1, 2}. The repeats vanish.

frames.label: grid = [[0] * 4 for _ in range(3)]
frames.say: [[0] * 4 for _ in range(3)] makes 3 rows of 4 zeros. Each turn of the loop builds a fresh row. _ means "unused".

frames.label: grid[1][2] = 5
frames.say: grid[1][2] = 5 sets row 1, column 2. The rows are separate lists, so only that one cell changes.

when: Transform every item of a list
Keep only the items that pass a test
Map each value to its index
Make an r by c grid or DP table
python:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
print([x * x for x in nums])
print([x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0])
print({x: i for i, x in enumerate(nums)})
print({x % 3 for x in nums})
grid = [[0] * 4 for _ in range(3)]
grid[1][2] = 5
for row in grid:
    print(row)
print([c for row in grid for c in row if c])
print(sum(x * x for x in nums))
watch: [[0] * 4] * 3 repeats one row three times, so a change shows in every row. Use the comprehension.
Two fors and two ifs in one comprehension is hard to read. Write a normal loop instead.
A list comprehension runs on every item. To stop at the first match, use a loop with break.
